strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: segmenting an image without requiring users to enumerate its categories. Automatically discovering a vocabulary could make segmentation more accessible and support recognition beyond fixed dataset taxonomies.

BCC offers a concrete technical idea: reuse the pretrained BLIP decoder to caption clustered subsets of image embeddings. Connecting these descriptions to an existing segmentation model is modular and requires no additional model training.

The experiments provide encouraging evidence for local category discovery. Table 1 improves class-agnostic mIoU over BLIP plus X-Decoder on all four datasets, including 71.8 versus 38.0 on VOC. Table 4 also reports substantial VOC gains over SAM- and LLaVA-based vocabulary generation using the same segmentor.

The overall pipeline is understandable, and the manuscript supplies hyperparameters, evaluator prompts, pseudocode, and a code link. The supplementary discussion constructively identifies failures involving compound nouns, competing category names, and scene confusion.
weaknesses: The central evaluator, LAVE, lacks validation against human mappings or alternative alignment methods. Appendix A relies on the LLM remembering the PC-459 and ADE20K vocabularies instead of supplying them. Its prompts also instruct the model to map stuff descriptions to background, although these benchmarks contain valid stuff classes. Algorithm 1's exact-name override only partly addresses this problem. A mapping audit and sensitivity analysis are needed to establish that reported mIoU reliably measures segmentation quality.

Table 3 does not establish comparable benchmark protocols. Its PC-459 column appears to contain PC-59 baseline results, such as OpenSeg's 45.9 and X-Decoder's 65.1, whereas AutoSeg explicitly evaluates 459 classes. It is also unclear whether ZeroSeg was rescored using LAVE. The comparison should reconcile label spaces and evaluators, and distinguish X-Decoder's inherited segmentation supervision from ZeroSeg's zero-segment-label setting before claiming a matched state-of-the-art improvement.

The model-selection protocol leaves uncertainty about generalization. Section 4.1 reports Bayesian optimization against VOC mIoU without identifying a separate tuning split, while Table 3 selects each dataset's best captioning-cycle count from Table 2. No repeated-run variability is reported despite stochastic caption generation. This matters particularly for small gains such as 11.7 versus 11.4 over LLaVA on Context in Table 4.

The ablations do not establish the contribution of several central BCC components. Table 1 tests broad pipeline variants, but there are no quantitative removals of multiscale processing, cross-clustering alignment, CRF refinement, or majority filtering. A local-captioning baseline with a matched caption budget would help establish how much the proposed refinements contribute. Furthermore, mapping predictions back to fixed categories does not validate the correctness of the finer-grained names highlighted in the qualitative examples.

Several implementation details need clarification for reproducibility. Equation 9 specifies independent maximum-IoU assignments rather than the stated one-to-one Hungarian matching; alignment between the 24×24 and 32×32 grids is unspecified; and the treatment of the appended 256-dimensional positional features before the frozen BLIP decoder is unclear. These are correctable description issues, but the evaluator and comparison concerns require substantive experimental verification.
